# Automated Aircraft Landing Guidance System: Detailed Description

## Overview of the Invention

The present invention relates to a method for automatically assisting the landing of an aircraft on a runway. This method provides comprehensive guidance for the aircraft throughout its approach sequence, beginning at an initial return point, designated as point (A), and concluding at a final completion point, designated as point (D), where the aircraft achieves touchdown on the runway surface. The entire guidance process is managed through an on-board data-processing device, which is operatively connected to both an altimeter and a deviation meter, enabling continuous monitoring and correction of the aircraft's flight parameters throughout the approach and landing sequence.

## Phase One: Return-Navigation Assistance

The first phase of the automated landing assistance method is the return-navigation phase, during which the aircraft is guided from the initial return point (A) toward the physical position of the deviation meter, identified as point (E). This guidance is accomplished through continuous measurement of azimuth deviations relative to a predetermined reference direction—specifically, the line connecting point (A) and point (E). By monitoring the aircraft's angular displacement from this reference line, the on-board data-processing device can generate the necessary corrective guidance commands to steer the aircraft along the intended trajectory toward the deviation meter's location, ensuring that the aircraft approaches the subsequent phase of the landing sequence with appropriate positional accuracy.

## Determination of the Capture Point

As the aircraft progresses along its guided trajectory, its position is precisely determined at a predetermined capture point, designated as point (B). This capture point is a critical transitional element within the overall guidance method, as it is specifically aligned with both the initial return point (A) and the deviation meter's position (E). This alignment ensures geometric consistency in the guidance solution, allowing the data-processing device to confirm that the aircraft has successfully completed the return-navigation phase and is properly positioned to transition into the subsequent stage of the landing sequence.

## Phase Two: Guidance to the Holding Point

Once the aircraft's position has been established at capture point (B), the method proceeds to guide the aircraft along a second predetermined path toward a holding point, designated as point (C). This holding point is selected such that it is approximately aligned with the axis of the runway, thereby establishing the aircraft on a trajectory that closely corresponds to the final approach path required for landing. During this segment of the guidance sequence, the on-board data-processing device utilizes multiple sources of flight data—specifically altitude information from the altimeter, heading data, and speed measurements—to accurately direct the aircraft along the prescribed path from point (B) to point (C). The integration of these three parameters allows for precise three-dimensional positioning of the aircraft as it transitions from the initial return-navigation phase toward final approach alignment.

## Phase Three: Landing Assistance and Final Completion

The final phase of the automated method is the landing assistance phase, which governs the guidance of the aircraft from the holding point (C) through to the completion point (D). During this concluding segment of the approach, the aircraft is progressively guided along its final descent path, with continuous adjustments made based on the ongoing data received from the altimeter and deviation meter. This phase culminates at completion point (D), which represents the point of touchdown, where the aircraft makes contact with the runway surface, thereby completing the automated landing sequence initiated at the return point (A).

## Summary of the Integrated Guidance Sequence

Taken together, these three distinct phases—the return-navigation phase (A to E, with position confirmation at B), the transitional guidance phase (B to C), and the landing assistance phase (C to D)—constitute a complete and continuous automated method for guiding an aircraft from its initial return point to final touchdown on the runway. By relying on the coordinated use of azimuth deviation measurements, altitude data, heading information, and speed parameters, the on-board data-processing device is able to maintain precise control over the aircraft's trajectory throughout each stage of the approach, ultimately ensuring a safe and accurate automated landing.

# AUTOMATED AIRCRAFT LANDING ASSISTANCE METHOD AND SYSTEM

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to the field of aircraft navigation and landing systems, and more particularly to an automated method for assisting aircraft during the approach and landing phases through the use of an on-board data-processing device operating in conjunction with an altimeter and a deviation meter.

## Background of the Invention

Modern aircraft landing operations require precise coordination between multiple flight parameters to ensure safe and accurate approach to the runway. Traditional landing assistance systems often rely heavily on pilot interpretation of instrument readings, which can introduce variability and potential error, particularly during periods of reduced visibility or challenging environmental conditions. There exists a continuing need for automated systems that can process navigational data in real time and guide the aircraft through a structured sequence of waypoints leading to a safe and stabilized landing.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention addresses these challenges by providing an automated aircraft landing assistance method that utilizes an on-board data-processing device connected to an altimeter and a deviation meter. This system is designed to guide the aircraft through a carefully structured, multi-phase return-navigation sequence, beginning at a designated return point and progressing through a series of defined waypoints until the aircraft reaches final approach alignment with the runway.

The method comprises a return-navigation phase during which the aircraft is guided from an initial return point toward a capture point. This capture point is defined and aligned according to a specific position indicated by the deviation meter, ensuring that the aircraft's lateral and vertical trajectory is properly registered with the intended approach path. From the capture point, the aircraft continues to a holding point, which is aligned with the runway axis itself, thereby establishing the final directional reference necessary for a stabilized landing approach.

Throughout this sequence, the on-board data-processing device continuously receives and processes multiple streams of flight data, including:

- **Azimuth deviation measurements**, which provide information regarding the aircraft's lateral offset relative to the intended flight path;
- **Altitude measurements**, obtained via the connected altimeter, which inform the vertical positioning of the aircraft relative to the required descent profile;
- **Heading measurements**, which indicate the aircraft's directional orientation; and
- **Speed measurements**, which are used to ensure that the aircraft maintains an appropriate velocity profile throughout each phase of the approach.

By integrating these four categories of measurement in real time, the data-processing device is able to calculate the necessary corrective commands and guidance signals required to move the aircraft smoothly and accurately from one waypoint to the next within the return-navigation sequence.

## Detailed Description of the Method

The automated landing assistance method proceeds according to the following general sequence:

**1. Initiation at the Return Point:** The aircraft begins the automated approach sequence at a predetermined return point, which serves as the initial reference location from which the return-navigation phase commences.

**2. Guidance to the Capture Point:** Using continuous azimuth deviation and altitude data, the on-board processing device calculates the necessary trajectory adjustments to guide the aircraft toward the capture point. This point is specifically defined by its alignment with a position registered by the deviation meter, ensuring that the aircraft is properly positioned relative to the approach corridor before proceeding further.

**3. Transition to the Holding Point:** Once the capture point has been reached and the aircraft's trajectory has been confirmed as properly aligned, the system guides the aircraft toward the holding point. This point is aligned with the runway axis, establishing the critical directional reference that will be maintained through the final approach and touchdown sequence.

**4. Continuous Monitoring and Correction:** Throughout each stage of this multi-point guidance sequence, the data-processing device continuously monitors heading and speed measurements, applying real-time corrections as necessary to maintain the aircraft within acceptable parameters for a safe and stabilized approach.

## Advantages of the Invention

This structured, multi-point guidance approach offers several significant advantages over conventional landing assistance methods. By automating the transition from the initial return point through the capture point and finally to the holding point, the invention enables a precise and repeatable approach sequence that reduces reliance on manual pilot intervention during critical phases of flight. The integration of azimuth deviation, altitude, heading, and speed data into a single coordinated processing system enhances overall navigational accuracy, ensuring that the aircraft remains properly aligned with the runway axis throughout the descent.

Furthermore, this automated approach contributes to improved safety outcomes during the critical descent and touchdown sequence, particularly under conditions where visual reference may be limited or where precise instrument-based guidance is essential. The invention's structured, sequential waypoint system also provides a clear and verifiable framework for evaluating the aircraft's progress through the approach phase, offering additional opportunities for system diagnostics and safety verification prior to touchdown.

## Conclusion

In summary, the present invention provides a comprehensive automated method for aircraft landing assistance that leverages on-board data-processing capabilities connected to an altimeter and deviation meter. Through a structured sequence of guidance points—from the return point, through the capture point, to the holding point aligned with the runway axis—the invention offers enhanced precision, consistency, and safety during one of the most critical phases of flight operations.

# The Word "The"

"The" is the most common word in the English language, appearing more frequently than any other. It is a definite article, used to specify particular nouns rather than general ones. When we say "the dog," we refer to a specific dog known to both speaker and listener, unlike "a dog," which refers to any dog in general.

Despite its small size—just three letters—"the" carries significant grammatical weight. It signals familiarity, specificity, and shared understanding between people communicating. Linguists note that articles like "the" don't exist in all languages; Russian, Japanese, and Mandarin Chinese, for example, manage perfectly well without them, using context and other grammatical structures to convey similar meaning.

The word traces its origins back to Old English, evolving from words like "þē" and "þæt," which were part of a larger system of pronouns and articles that has simplified considerably over the centuries. Today, "the" remains remarkably stable, used identically whether preceding singular or plural nouns, unlike many other parts of English grammar that shift and change with number and case.

Interestingly, "the" also appears in phrases and idioms that stretch beyond simple grammatical function. "The" can imply something quintessential or superlative, as in "he is the expert" or "this is the place to be," suggesting singularity and importance beyond mere specification.

For writers, "the" is often invisible—it rarely draws attention to itself, yet its presence or absence can change the tone and meaning of a sentence. Removing articles altogether, as some poets do for stylistic effect, produces a stripped-down, almost telegraphic quality to language, highlighting just how much subtle work "the" performs in ordinary speech and writing.

In essence, while "the" might seem like a mundane grammatical tool, it serves as a quiet architect of meaning, shaping how we understand specificity, shared knowledge, and even importance within the vast landscape of the English language.

processing said altitude data and said deviation data via a processing unit operatively coupled to said altimeter and said deviation meter, said processing unit executing a stored algorithm configured to compute, at a predetermined sampling rate, a corrective guidance signal indicative of a required adjustment to at least one of aircraft pitch, roll, and thrust necessary to reduce said lateral and vertical deviation while maintaining a target descent profile; # TECHNICAL BACKGROUND

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to aircraft guidance and navigation systems, and more particularly to systems and methods for providing autonomous approach and landing guidance to aircraft without reliance on ground-based precision approach infrastructure.

## Background of the Invention

Modern commercial and military aircraft rely heavily on precision approach and landing systems to safely execute landings, particularly under conditions of reduced visibility such as fog, heavy precipitation, or nighttime operations. Historically, the aviation industry has depended on ground-based infrastructure, most notably the Instrument Landing System (ILS), to provide the lateral and vertical guidance necessary for aircraft to align with a runway and descend along a safe glidepath to touchdown.

While ILS has served as the primary precision approach aid for decades, it suffers from several well-documented limitations. ILS installations require significant capital investment in ground transmitter equipment, antenna arrays, and monitoring systems at each runway end to be served. This infrastructure is susceptible to signal multipath interference caused by nearby buildings, terrain, or even other taxiing aircraft, and requires designated critical areas to be kept clear during low-visibility operations, thereby reducing airport throughput. Furthermore, ILS signals are subject to a finite number of available frequency channels, limiting the number of simultaneous approaches that can be supported in high-density terminal areas. Many smaller airports and remote airfields lack ILS installations entirely due to the cost of installation and maintenance, leaving aircraft without precision guidance capability during adverse weather conditions.

Satellite-based augmentation systems (SBAS) and ground-based augmentation systems (GBAS) have been developed to provide GPS-based approach guidance as an alternative to ILS. However, these systems remain dependent on external signal sources that may be subject to jamming, spoofing, signal degradation, or outright unavailability in certain geographic regions or during periods of atmospheric disturbance. Reliance on Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals introduces vulnerabilities in contested or electromagnetically degraded environments, a concern of particular significance in military aviation applications, but increasingly relevant to civil aviation resilience planning as well.

Autonomous sensor-based approaches, including those utilizing millimeter-wave radar, LIDAR, and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) imaging systems, have been proposed as means of providing landing guidance independent of ground infrastructure and satellite signals. However, prior art systems in this domain have generally suffered from one or more of the following deficiencies: (1) insufficient accuracy in runway edge and centerline detection under degraded visual conditions such as fog, smoke, blowing sand, or heavy precipitation; (2) inability to reliably distinguish the intended runway from adjacent taxiways, other runways, or similar linear features in complex airport environments; (3) excessive computational latency between sensor data acquisition and guidance command generation, resulting in guidance solutions that lag the aircraft's actual dynamic state; (4) lack of robust sensor fusion architectures capable of gracefully degrading performance when one or more sensor modalities become compromised, rather than failing outright; and (5) inadequate integration with aircraft flight control systems to translate sensor-derived positional data into stable, certifiable guidance commands compatible with existing autopilot and flight director architectures.

Additionally, existing autonomous landing approaches have generally failed to adequately address the integrity monitoring requirements necessary for certification under applicable aviation safety standards, such as those promulgated by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). Systems intended to provide guidance during critical phases of flight must incorporate robust fault detection, exclusion, and annunciation capabilities to ensure that erroneous guidance is not presented to the flight crew or automated flight control system without timely warning.

There exists, therefore, a need for an autonomous approach and landing guidance system that: does not depend on ground-based transmitters or continuous availability of satellite navigation signals; provides accurate, low-latency runway identification and relative position determination under a wide range of environmental and visibility conditions; incorporates redundant sensing modalities with robust fusion and fault-tolerant architectures; and generates guidance outputs compatible with existing aircraft flight control and display systems in a manner suitable for airworthiness certification. The present invention addresses these needs, as described in greater detail in the following sections.

# METHOD FOR GUIDING AN AIRCRAFT FROM A RETURN POINT THROUGH CAPTURE AND HOLDING POINTS TO TOUCHDOWN

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates to systems and methods for aircraft navigation and landing guidance, and more particularly to a method for guiding an aircraft along a predetermined trajectory from an initial return point, through defined capture and holding points, to a touchdown point using azimuth deviation and altitude measurements.

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Precision approach and landing systems require reliable guidance of an aircraft along a controlled path to ensure safe touchdown at a designated location on a runway. Conventional systems often rely on ground-based instrument landing systems (ILS) or satellite-based navigation, which may be subject to signal degradation, interference, or unavailability in certain operational environments. There exists a need for a robust guidance method that utilizes onboard or relative azimuth deviation and altitude measurements to guide an aircraft through a structured sequence of navigational points, ensuring accurate and repeatable approach and landing performance.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention provides a method for guiding an aircraft comprising the steps of determining a return point associated with the aircraft's current position and flight parameters; computing a guidance trajectory from the return point to a capture point; transitioning the aircraft onto an approach path upon reaching the capture point; maintaining the aircraft at a holding point when required by traffic, operational, or procedural conditions; and subsequently guiding the aircraft along a final approach path to a touchdown point, wherein guidance at each stage is performed based at least in part on azimuth deviation measurements and altitude measurements obtained during flight.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### 1. Overview of the Guidance Sequence

In accordance with one embodiment of the invention, a method is provided for guiding an aircraft (10) from a return point (RP) through a capture point (CP) and, optionally, a holding point (HP), to a touchdown point (TD) on a landing surface. The method comprises a sequence of navigational phases, each characterized by distinct guidance computations based on azimuth deviation and altitude data.

### 2. Determination of the Return Point

The return point (RP) is defined as a predetermined or dynamically computed geographic position at which the aircraft initiates or resumes guided navigation toward the landing area. The return point may be established based on one or more of: (a) a predefined waypoint stored in a navigation database; (b) a position calculated relative to a reference station using azimuth and distance measurements; or (c) a position determined by onboard sensors including, without limitation, inertial navigation systems, satellite positioning receivers, or radio navigation aids.

Upon determining the aircraft's current position relative to the return point, an azimuth deviation signal is generated, representing an angular difference between the aircraft's actual bearing and a desired bearing toward the capture point. Concurrently, an altitude measurement is obtained representing the aircraft's current height above a reference datum, such as mean sea level or the landing surface elevation.

### 3. Guidance from Return Point to Capture Point

The method further comprises computing a first guidance trajectory extending from the return point to the capture point (CP). This computation includes:

(a) determining an azimuth deviation between the aircraft's instantaneous heading and a reference azimuth line extending from the return point to the capture point;

(b) generating steering commands, based on the azimuth deviation, to correct the aircraft's heading toward the reference azimuth line;

(c) monitoring altitude throughout the transit segment to ensure compliance with a predetermined altitude profile associated with the return-point-to-capture-point segment; and

(d) adjusting the aircraft's rate of descent or ascent, as necessary, based on a deviation between the measured altitude and a target altitude value defined for the aircraft's along-path position.

The capture point (CP) is defined as a position at which the aircraft intercepts a predetermined approach path, such as an extended runway centerline or a defined glide path. Upon reaching the capture point, the method transitions to a capture phase, wherein the aircraft's guidance system aligns the aircraft's trajectory with the approach path based on continuously updated azimuth deviation and altitude measurements.

### 4. Optional Holding Point Procedure

In certain embodiments, the method further comprises directing the aircraft to a holding point (HP) when conditions require a delay prior to final approach. The holding point may be defined by a predetermined geographic coordinate, azimuth bearing, and altitude range relative to the capture point or touchdown point.

While at the holding point, the method comprises:

(a) maintaining the aircraft within a bounded holding pattern by iteratively computing azimuth deviation relative to a reference holding course;

(b) maintaining the aircraft within a predetermined altitude band based on continuous altitude measurements; and

(c) upon receipt of a clearance signal or satisfaction of a predetermined condition, terminating the holding procedure and resuming guidance toward the touchdown point.

It will be appreciated that the holding point procedure is optional and may be omitted in embodiments where direct transition from the capture point to final approach is appropriate.

### 5. Final Approach and Touchdown Guidance

Following the capture phase, or the holding point procedure where applicable, the method further comprises guiding the aircraft along a final approach path to the touchdown point (TD). This final guidance phase comprises:

(a) continuously measuring an azimuth deviation between the aircraft's instantaneous position and a final approach course extending toward the touchdown point;

(b) continuously measuring the aircraft's altitude relative to a target descent profile, such as a predetermined glide slope angle;

(c) generating lateral guidance commands as a function of the azimuth deviation to maintain the aircraft on the final approach course;

(d) generating vertical guidance commands as a function of a deviation between the measured altitude and the target descent profile; and

(e) upon the aircraft reaching a predetermined altitude threshold or along-path position proximate the touchdown point, generating a flare command to reduce the aircraft's rate of descent for touchdown.

### 6. Guidance Signal Generation and Control

In accordance with further embodiments, the azimuth deviation and altitude measurements described above may be derived from one or more onboard sensors, including without limitation an inertial reference unit, a radio altimeter, a barometric altimeter, a satellite navigation receiver, or a ground-based azimuth reference transmitter in communication with an onboard receiver.

The method may further comprise generating steering and descent commands as electrical signals communicated to an autopilot system, a flight director display, or a flight management computer, such that the aircraft may be guided automatically, semi-automatically, or manually by a pilot referencing the guidance commands.

### 7. Alternative Embodiments

In alternative embodiments, the sequence of navigational points may include additional intermediate points beyond the return point, capture point, holding point, and touchdown point, without departing from the scope of the invention. Furthermore, the specific measurements used for guidance may include additional parameters such as ground speed, vertical speed, or wind correction angle, in combination with the azimuth deviation and altitude measurements described herein.

## CLAIMS (Exemplary)

**1.** A method for guiding an aircraft from a return point to a touchdown point, the method comprising:
determining a return point associated with a current position of the aircraft;
generating a first azimuth deviation signal representing a deviation between an instantaneous heading of the aircraft and a reference azimuth extending toward a capture point;
guiding the aircraft from the return point to the capture point based at least in part on the first azimuth deviation signal and a first altitude measurement;
upon the aircraft reaching the capture point, transitioning the aircraft onto an approach path;
guiding the aircraft along the approach path toward a touchdown point based at least in part on a second azimuth deviation signal and a second altitude measurement; and
generating a flare command as the aircraft approaches the touchdown point to reduce a rate of descent of the aircraft.

**2.** The method of claim 1, further comprising directing the aircraft to a holding point prior to guiding the aircraft toward the touchdown point, wherein the aircraft is maintained within a predetermined azimuth and altitude range at the holding point until a clearance condition is satisfied.

**3.** The method of claim 1, wherein the first altitude measurement and the second altitude measurement are obtained from at least one of a radio altimeter, a barometric altimeter, or a satellite navigation receiver.

**4.** The method of claim 1, wherein the first azimuth deviation signal and the second azimuth deviation signal are derived from a ground-based azimuth reference transmitter in communication with an onboard receiver of the aircraft.

**5.** The method of claim 1, further comprising generating steering commands communicated to an autopilot system of the aircraft based on the first and second azimuth deviation signals.

**6.** The method of claim 1, further comprising generating descent rate commands based on a deviation between the first altitude measurement or the second altitude measurement and a predetermined target altitude profile.

---

# SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR TWO-PHASE AUTOMATIC AIRCRAFT GUIDANCE

## [0001] Technical Field and Summary of the Invention

In accordance with an exemplary embodiment, there is provided an automatic aircraft guidance system configured to autonomously direct an aircraft from a mission-interrupted or off-nominal flight condition to a safe landing at a designated recovery airfield through two sequentially executed operational phases: a return-navigation phase and a landing phase. The system comprises a navigation processor, a flight management module operatively coupled to aircraft flight control surfaces and propulsion systems, and a guidance logic unit configured to compute, sequence, and transition between a plurality of defined waypoints, referred to herein as the return point, the capture point, the holding point, and the completion point, each serving a distinct navigational function within the overall guidance sequence.

The **return point** is defined as a first navigational waypoint, computed by the guidance logic unit in response to a triggering event—including, without limitation, loss of command link, low fuel state, adverse weather detection, or operator-initiated recovery command—representing the initial target position toward which the aircraft is automatically commanded upon entry into the return-navigation phase, said return point being selected based on aircraft current position, heading, altitude, and airspace constraints so as to establish an initial great-circle or dynamically-computed course toward the recovery airfield.

The **capture point** is defined as a second navigational waypoint disposed along the return-navigation flight path, at or beyond which the guidance logic unit transitions aircraft control from the return-navigation phase to the landing phase, said capture point being positioned relative to the recovery airfield such that the aircraft's position, altitude, and airspeed at the time of arrival satisfy predetermined entry criteria for engagement of a precision approach guidance mode, including, in certain embodiments, an instrument landing system beam, a satellite-based augmentation trajectory, or an onboard vision-based guidance solution.

The **holding point** is defined as a navigational waypoint, computed and, in certain embodiments, dynamically recomputed by the guidance logic unit, at which the aircraft is commanded to enter a loitering or racetrack holding pattern in the event that landing clearance has not been received, runway occupancy is detected, or environmental conditions preclude immediate approach, the aircraft remaining at the holding point for a variable duration until the guidance logic unit determines that conditions are satisfied for resumption of the landing phase.

The **completion point** is defined as a terminal waypoint or condition, located proximate the runway surface or at a predetermined altitude above ground level, at which the automatic guidance system determines that the landing phase has been successfully concluded, including, in various embodiments, touchdown detection via radar altimeter, weight-on-wheels sensor activation, or deceleration below a threshold ground speed, whereupon the guidance logic unit terminates automatic guidance authority and transfers control to a ground-operations or taxi-control subsystem.

## [0002] Detailed Description of Operation

In operation, upon detection of a triggering event, the guidance logic unit computes the return point and commands the aircraft thereto, thereby initiating the return-navigation phase, during which the aircraft is guided along a computed course, subject to continuous monitoring of airspace deconfliction, terrain avoidance, and fuel-remaining constraints, toward the capture point. Upon arrival at or satisfaction of criteria associated with the capture point, the guidance logic unit automatically transitions aircraft control authority to the landing phase, wherein the aircraft is guided along a precision approach trajectory toward the recovery airfield, subject to diversion, as necessary, to the holding point should landing clearance or environmental conditions be unfavorable at the time of approach. Upon satisfaction of clearance and environmental criteria, the aircraft is automatically redirected from the holding point to resume the approach trajectory, culminating in arrival at the completion point, whereupon automatic guidance is terminated and control is transferred to a subsequent operational subsystem. It will be appreciated by one of ordinary skill in the art that the foregoing waypoints may be computed, in various embodiments, in real time based on sensor data, updated telemetry, or operator input, and that the sequence and number of waypoints may be varied without departing from the scope of the present invention.
